records.place: Serdiana, Isola dei Nuraghi IGT, southern Sardinia

wine.name: Turriga
wine.classification: IGT, the geographic indication below DOC and DOCG
wine.grapes: Cannonau, the great majority, with small parts of Carignano, Bovale Sardo and Malvasia Nera, all from the Turriga vineyard.
wine.sites: The Turriga vineyard at about 230 metres between Selegas and Piscina Trigus, north of Cagliari, on moderately limestone soils with gravel and sand.
wine.making: Fermented warm, at 28 to 32 degrees Celsius, with some sixteen to eighteen days on the skins and délestage, the juice drained off and returned over the cap. It then ages for 18 to 24 months in French oak barriques and rests about a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and myrtle with dried Mediterranean herbs, liquorice and a toasty note from the barriques; full, warm and dense, with ripe, firm tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and marked by oak when young, it wants five years and more in bottle; it was conceived for long keeping, and good vintages last for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead and an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The locality near Selegas that names the vineyard, where a prehistoric marble statuette of a mother goddess was found, by the house's account.
The geographic indication whose zone is the whole of Sardinia, wider than any DOC of the island.
The tier below DOC, which leaves the house free to set its own blend and ageing.

records.table: Turriga is Argiolas's red from a single vineyard near Selegas: Cannonau with small parts of Carignano, Bovale Sardo and Malvasia Nera, aged up to two years in French barriques. Dark, warm and firm, with black cherry and myrtle, it wants a decanter when young.
records.story: The Argiolas family grew grapes at Serdiana, north of Cagliari, and by the house's account its story as a cellar begins in 1938, when the founder, born in 1906, inherited a small vineyard from his father. For some fifty years the house sold most of its wine in bulk. A journey to Argentina and California in 1979, as the house tells it, showed the founder the worth of joining scattered plots into larger vineyards, and he went on to buy estates at Selegas. In 1988 the house began working with the oenologist Giacomo Tachis (1933 to 2016), the maker of Tignanello and adviser to Sassicaia, with one aim: a long lived Sardinian red from the island's own grapes alone. The first harvest of Turriga was picked that year, and the wine was first released in 1991. Its vineyard and its name come from a locality near Selegas where, the house says, a marble statuette of a mother goddess more than five thousand years old was found. The third generation took the house on in 2003, and the founder died in 2009, past the age of a hundred. For a sommelier Turriga is the bottle that showed, from the late 1980s, that Cannonau and its island companions could make a Sardinian red for the cellar.

others.name: Korem
others.note: A red led by Bovale with Carignano and Cannonau, the house's second blend of island grapes, also Isola dei Nuraghi IGT.

others.name: Costera
others.note: The house's Cannonau, from the grape that leads Turriga.

others.name: Costamolino
others.note: The house's widely poured white, a Vermentino di Sardegna DOC.

traps: Turriga is an Isola dei Nuraghi IGT, not a Cannonau di Sardegna DOC: it is a blend of four island grapes aged in French barriques.
Turriga names a locality near Selegas where the vineyard lies, not a grape or a village; the winery itself is at Serdiana.
Cannonau, Turriga's main grape, is Grenache, and Carignano is Carignan; Bovale Sardo and Malvasia Nera are the small parts.

cards.front: Argiolas: where is the Turriga vineyard, and what is its soil?
cards.back: Near Selegas at about 230 metres, on moderately limestone soils with gravel and sand.

cards.front: Which oenologist shaped Turriga with the Argiolas family, and when was its first harvest?
cards.back: Giacomo Tachis (1933 to 2016); the first harvest came in 1988 and the wine was released in 1991.

questions.q: A guest asks which grape leads the blend of Argiolas's Turriga. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Cannonau, Sardinia's name for Grenache, is the great majority of Turriga; Carignano, Bovale Sardo and Malvasia Nera make up small parts of the blend.

questions.q: Argiolas sold most of its wine in bulk for some fifty years. Which oenologist helped the family create Turriga, first harvested in 1988?
questions.exp: Tachis, the oenologist of Tignanello, worked with the family from 1988 on a long lived red of island grapes; Émile Peynaud was a Bordeaux oenologist with no part in Turriga.

Argiolas: Eine Familiengeschichte, the family history

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35 (one wasted on an Italian search for the founder's death), plus one shared with Capichera for the Isola dei Nuraghi disciplinare and one shared with Santadi for Giacomo Tachis's dates (Wikipedia, Scatti di Gusto and The Drinks Business, cited in Santadi's sources for the cap of five); the house's own pages were read through search.

The plan's note is answered: the house gives 1988 as Turriga's first harvest and 1991 as its release; Winebow and Vinous give about 85 per cent Cannonau with some 5 per cent each of Carignano, Bovale Sardo and Malvasia Nera (Vinous: the minor parts vary by vintage), and the house's German history page names the same four; the label is Isola dei Nuraghi IGT on the house's own page.

The founder is Antonio Argiolas, born in 1906 by the house's Turriga page and dead in 2009 at 102 (Italian Tribune, WineNews; one trade article says 103); he is described, not named, because his grandson of the same name is living, so a bare Antonio Argiolas in people.json would otherwise trip a dated mention.

The site rests on the house's German page (Selegas and Piscina Trigus at 230 metres) and its product page (medium limestone), with Vinous for gravel and sand; Vinous alone says the family's oldest Cannonau grows there, so that is cut, and the house alone says the Selegas estates became its largest, also cut.

Making from the house's Turriga page: 28 to 32 degrees Celsius, 16 to 18 days' maceration with délestage, 18 to 24 months in French barriques and 12 to 14 in bottle; Winebow gives two years in French barriques.

Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: the grandchildren Valentina, Francesca and Antonio Argiolas, the technical director Mariano Murru and a trade spokesman Beppe Pinna; the founder's sons Franco and Giuseppe are not named, their status unsettled.

Library: p-argiolas agrees (1938, the four grapes, Tachis); the region record's Turriga line calls it the wine that showed Sardinia could make a world class red, a superlative this record does not repeat.

records.place: I Piani, Alghero, Alghero DOC, north western Sardinia

wine.name: Terre Bianche Cuvée 161
wine.grapes: Torbato alone, a rare white grape of Alghero that the house, by its own account, rediscovered and brought back.
wine.sites: The house's own vineyards on the estate at I Piani, north of Alghero; Terre Bianche, white earths, names the pale soils rich in limestone.
wine.making: The grapes are chilled and left on their skins for a short cold maceration, then pressed softly and fermented cool in stainless steel. The wine rests on its lees for about six months, mostly in steel with a small part in barriques, and does not go through malolactic fermentation.
wine.glass: Mediterranean scrub, thistle and medicinal herbs with a hint of citrus peel; smooth at first, then savoury and almost salty, of medium body, with fresh acidity and a light touch of the barrique.
wine.ageing: Fresh and open on release, it keeps well for a few years after the vintage, growing rounder and more savoury.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: The Alghero DOC of the island's north west, with Torbato named as the grape.
White earths, for the pale, limestone rich soils of the vineyard.
The house's selected bottling of Torbato, set above its other wines of the grape.

records.table: Terre Bianche Cuvée 161 is Sella & Mosca's Torbato from Alghero, a rare white grape the house says it brought back, fermented cool in steel with a small part rested in barriques. Savoury, almost salty, with Mediterranean scrub and thistle, it suits the lobster and fish of that coast.
records.story: In 1899 two Piedmontese, an engineer of the Sella family and a lawyer of the Mosca family, bought a great tract of marshy, uncultivated land at I Piani, north of Alghero, and set about reclaiming it. Phylloxera was then ruining the vineyards of Europe, and the estate began as a nursery of young vines grafted on American rootstocks, to replant the stricken vineyards of the mainland; at its heart, by the house's account, stood a workshop for grafting and forcing cuttings. In 1903 a Neolithic necropolis was found on the estate's land, Anghelu Ruju, whose name the house later gave to its sweet red. In time the nursery became a wine estate on its own vineyards, and it took up Torbato, a rare white grape that, by its own account, it rediscovered and brought back to the market. The estate passed to the Campari group in 2002 and to the Terra Moretti group in 2016. For a sommelier Terre Bianche is the bottle that puts Torbato, and the Alghero DOC, on a wine list: a savoury coastal white of a rare grape.

others.name: Anghelu Ruju
others.note: Alghero Liquoroso Riserva: Cannonau dried in the sun on reed mats, fortified and aged at least seven years in oak, named for the necropolis.

others.name: Marchese di Villamarina
others.note: Alghero Cabernet Riserva DOC: Cabernet Sauvignon alone, long on its skins, then aged in barriques.

traps: Torbato is the grape and Terre Bianche the name of the wine; the appellation on the label is Alghero, a DOC of the island's north west.
Anghelu Ruju is a fortified sweet red of sun dried Cannonau, not a dry Cannonau di Sardegna.

cards.front: Sella & Mosca: which grape makes Terre Bianche, and what appellation does it carry?
cards.back: Torbato alone, a rare white grape; Alghero Torbato DOC.

cards.front: What was found on the Sella & Mosca estate in 1903, and which wine takes its name?
cards.back: The Neolithic necropolis of Anghelu Ruju; the house's sweet, fortified Cannonau carries its name.

questions.q: A guest orders Sella & Mosca's Terre Bianche Cuvée 161 and asks what grape it is. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Terre Bianche is Torbato alone, a rare white grape of Alghero; Vermentino is the island's main white, used for Vermentino di Gallura and Vermentino di Sardegna.

questions.q: Sella & Mosca was founded near Alghero in 1899. What did the estate first do on its reclaimed land?
opts: Grafted young vines on American rootstocks
Grew cork oaks for the bottle trade
questions.exp: Phylloxera was ruining Europe's vineyards, and the estate began as a nursery of vines grafted on resistant American rootstocks; its wine estate came later.

sources.title: Sella & Mosca: la tenuta, the estate
Sella & Mosca: Terre Bianche Cuvée 161 technical sheet
Sella & Mosca: Anghelu Ruju technical sheet
WineNews: Sella & Mosca, 120 years of Italian wine
WineNews: Terra Moretti buys Sella & Mosca from Campari

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 35, the house's pages and technical sheets read through search, with WineNews (two articles) and On Magazine for the nursery and the sales.

The plan's note is answered: the house's English page heads the wine Terre Bianche Cuvée 161, Alghero Torbato DOC, and calls it the fullest expression of its Torbato (its Italian page heads it Cuvée 161); a plain Terre Bianche of steel appears on older merchants' lists, so the record teaches the Cuvée 161, which holds the plan's words. What 161 stands for is not on the house's pages; one merchant says a block of the Terre Bianche vineyard, left out.

The Torbato claim: the house's own sheet calls it a rare variety rediscovered and rehabilitated by Sella & Mosca, which the record hedges; the plan's why (a grape the house long grew almost alone) rests on one merchant's claim that it is the only producer still planting it in Sardinia, and is not repeated.

The two founders are described, not named: the house's reports and WineNews name the engineer Erminio Sella and the lawyer Edgardo Mosca, but no source searched gave their dates, and sources disagree on Sella's tie to the statesman Quintino Sella (grandson or nephew) and one gives his first name as Emilio.

The nursery of grafted vines on American rootstocks rests on WineNews (marshy land at I Piani reclaimed for a nursery of barbatelle) and On Magazine, beside the house's own page on its grafting workshop; the first vineyards of 1901 and the winery of 1903 rest on one source and are left out.

The necropolis found in 1903 rests on the house's Anghelu Ruju sheet and Sardegna Turismo, the region's own site (found while a farmhouse was dug; the Ozieri culture, late Neolithic), not in the sources for the cap of five; Campari's purchase of 2002 and the sale to Terra Moretti in 2016 rest on WineNews, L'Unione Sarda and the house's own page.

The two sheets of Cuvée 161 differ (12 or 24 hours of cold maceration, part fermented in barrique or about 15 per cent aged there), so the making says a small part in barriques; Marchese di Villamarina's sheets disagree on months in barrique (14 or 18), left out.
Living names met, none in the fragment: the owner of Terra Moretti, already in people.json; no library record holds the house, so nothing is in tension.

records.place: Cabras, on the gulf of Oristano, Vernaccia di Oristano DOC, Sardinia

wine.name: Antico Gregori
wine.classification: Riserva of the Vernaccia di Oristano DOC, Sardinia's first DOC, decreed in 1971
wine.grapes: Vernaccia di Oristano alone, a white grape of the lower Tirso valley, unrelated to the Vernaccia of San Gimignano.
wine.sites: Vineyards of the lower Tirso valley and the Sinis peninsula around Cabras, on the lean, sandy soil called gregori, which gives the wine its name.
wine.making: Picked in mid October and pressed softly, the Vernaccia ferments as a white wine, then ages for decades in small casks of oak and chestnut kept part filled, where a film of flor forms. For the release of the 1991, by the house's sheet, some thirty three years of oxidative ageing were freshened with a little much older Vernaccia.
wine.glass: Bright amber with old gold glints; hazelnut, honey, walnut husk and custard, closing on salted peanut and fig; dry, savoury and very long, with no sweetness at all.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink after decades in cask; a stable, oxidative wine, it keeps for many years in bottle.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, as the house advises, cool rather than cold; no need to decant; a large white wine glass, poured in small measures.

label.means: The DOC of the Tirso valley and the gulf of Oristano for Vernaccia aged in wood, decreed in 1971.
The DOC's longer aged type, held for years in cask before release.
Old Gregori, after the lean, sandy soil of the Tirso valley that the grape is grown on.

records.table: Antico Gregori is Attilio Contini's long aged Vernaccia di Oristano, kept for decades at Cabras in part filled casks under flor and never fortified: dry, amber and savoury, with walnut, honey and fig. Pour it cool in a large glass, beside bottarga, as the house suggests.
records.story: Vernaccia was the common wine of the gulf of Oristano when the Contini family, whose roots in Cabras go back by its own account to a marriage recorded in 1642, began to make and sell it in 1898. The founder, Salvatore Contini, set out to raise the standing of the district's wine, and after his death in 1936 the cellar passed to his son Attilio, whose name the house took. In 1971 Vernaccia di Oristano became the first wine of Sardinia to receive a DOC, by a decree of 11 August that year. The family's long reserves of old wine gave rise to Antico Gregori. The house once described it as a cuvée built in the solera manner on a base wine of the early twentieth century, topped up only with chosen vintages; later releases carry the year of their harvest, among them the 1976, the 1979 and the 1991, each aged for decades. For a sommelier Antico Gregori is the reference for Vernaccia di Oristano: an unfortified white aged for decades in part filled casks, under flor and then air, close in spirit to an old dry Sherry.

others.name: Vernaccia di Oristano Riserva
others.note: The house's classic Riserva, aged for many years, by its sheet, in part filled casks of oak and chestnut so that flor forms.

others.name: Vernaccia di Oristano Flor
others.note: The house's younger Vernaccia, aged some years in small casks under flor: the way into the style.

traps: Vernaccia di Oristano is unrelated to Vernaccia di San Gimignano, the Tuscan white, and to Vernaccia di Serrapetrona, a sparkling red of the Marche.
Antico Gregori is a Riserva and is not fortified; the fortified Vernaccia is the DOC's liquoroso type.
Serve Antico Gregori cool, at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius as the house advises, not chilled like a Fino.

cards.front: Attilio Contini: in what casks does its Vernaccia di Oristano age, and under what?
cards.back: Small casks of oak and chestnut, kept part filled so that a film of flor yeast forms on the wine.

cards.front: In which year did Vernaccia di Oristano become Sardinia's first DOC, and which Contini wine is its long aged Riserva?

questions.q: A guest tastes Attilio Contini's Antico Gregori and asks how it was aged. Which answer fits?
opts: Decades in part filled casks under flor
Two years in new French barriques
A year in steel, then in bottle
Months in clay amphorae on the skins
questions.exp: Antico Gregori ages for decades in small part filled casks of oak and chestnut, where flor forms and air slowly works on the wine; new barriques would give vanilla and toast instead.

questions.q: Vernaccia di Oristano, the wine Contini built its name on, was the first Sardinian wine to receive a DOC. In which year?
questions.exp: The DOC was decreed in August 1971, the island's first; 1898 is the year the house dates its founding to, and 1996 the year Vermentino di Gallura became a DOCG.

Contini: Antico Gregori, Vernaccia di Oristano DOC Riserva, technical sheet
AIS: disciplinare of the Vernaccia di Oristano DOC
L'Unione Sarda: Cantina Contini 1898 at Wine Paris 2026
Gambero Rosso: Antico Gregori 1976

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35 and the group's one fetch (the house's Antico Gregori sheet on vinicontini.com, refused: the host does not resolve here); the house's pages and sheets were read through search.

The plan's note is answered: the house's older English page calls Antico Gregori a cuvée in the solera manner on a base wine of the early 1900s topped up with chosen vintages, while its sheet of April 2025 is for the 1991 vintage (some 33 years of oxidative ageing, with small amounts of very old Vernaccia, above all the 1975), and Gambero Rosso writes of the 1976 and the 1979; so recent releases carry a vintage and the label reads Vernaccia di Oristano DOC Riserva.

Library tension: p-attilio-contini's wines note says Antico Gregori is blended from very old reserves, true of the older bottlings and only in part of the vintage dated releases; its why calls Vernaccia di Oristano the only Italian wine matured under flor, while the region record says Malvasia di Bosa is made in the same flor tradition, so the record makes no claim of an only.

The first Sardinian DOC of 1971 rests on the house's history page and Dissapore (prima DOC riconosciuta della Sardegna), with the decree of 11 August 1971 in the AIS copy of the disciplinare; Dissapore is not in the sources for the cap of five.

Salvatore Contini is named with his death alone (1936, by the house's history), since no source gave his birth; the award notice of 2025 names Anna Maria Dessì as co-founder, left out for want of her dates and a second source; the gold medal at Milan in 1912 rests on the house alone and is left out.

The serving temperature of 16 to 18 degrees Celsius in a large glass is the house's own; the Riserva's minimum years in wood (four by Dissapore, not read in the decree) are left out of the label, which says held for years.

The house now presents itself as Contini 1898 while Gambero Rosso and older labels carry Attilio Contini; the plan's producer is kept. Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Alessandro Contini and Mauro Contini, the fourth generation.

records.place: Santadi, Sulcis, Carignano del Sulcis DOC, south western Sardinia

wine.name: Terre Brune
wine.classification: Superiore of the Carignano del Sulcis DOC, from bush trained vines alone
wine.grapes: Carignano, nearly all of it, with a little Bovale Sardo, known locally as Bovaleddu.
wine.sites: Old vineyards of the lower Sulcis, bush trained and on their own roots, in loose sandy and calcareous soils near the sea, where phylloxera could not take hold.
wine.making: Picked by hand from late September to mid October and fermented on the skins in temperature controlled stainless steel for about fifteen days. An early malolactic fermentation lets the wine go into fine grained French oak barriques by early December, where it ages for about eighteen months before bottling.
wine.glass: Deep ruby with garnet glints; plum, bilberry, bay leaf and juniper with tobacco and dark chocolate; full and smooth, with soft, ripe tannin, a salty, iodine note and a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Generous on release, it gains savoury depth over a decade in bottle and keeps longer in strong vintages.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead and an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The DOC of Sardinia's south western corner, for reds of at least 85 per cent Carignano.
The DOC's higher type, which must come only from bush trained vines, the alberello.
The co-operative of growers at Santadi, founded in 1960, which makes and bottles the wine.

records.table: Terre Brune is Cantina Santadi's Carignano del Sulcis Superiore: old bush vines on their own roots in the sand of the Sulcis, with a little Bovaleddu, aged some eighteen months in French barriques. Dark, smooth and savoury, with plum and bay leaf, it wants a decanter young.
records.story: In 1960 grape growers at Santadi, in the Sulcis of south western Sardinia, joined together in a co-operative, and for years it sold its wine in bulk. From the middle of the 1970s, as the co-operative tells it, it turned to bottled wine of quality and brought in Giacomo Tachis (1933 to 2016), the oenologist of Tignanello, who had come to the island to advise its consortium of DOC wines. Tachis saw what the Sulcis held: old Carignano grown as bush vines on their own roots in coastal sand, where phylloxera had never taken hold. He asked for lower yields and strict selection of the grapes, and in 1984 the co-operative made the first Terre Brune, by its own account the first Sardinian red of real structure aged in barriques. The Carignano del Sulcis DOC dated from 1977, and the rule that its Superiore must come from bush vines alone makes the old alberello the heart of the wine. For a sommelier Terre Brune is the proof that a co-operative can make its region's reference red, and that old Carignano on its own roots can make a wine for the cellar.

others.name: Rocca Rubia
others.note: Carignano del Sulcis Riserva, the step beneath Terre Brune in the co-operative's range.

traps: Terre Brune is a Superiore of the Carignano del Sulcis DOC; Sardinia's one DOCG is Vermentino di Gallura, in the north east.
Carignano is Carignan; in the Sulcis it grows on its own roots, because phylloxera cannot spread through the sand.
Cantina Santadi is a co-operative of growers, not a family estate; Rocca Rubia is its Riserva beneath Terre Brune.

cards.front: Cantina Santadi: why are the Carignano vines of Terre Brune on their own roots?
cards.back: They grow in sandy soil near the sea, through which phylloxera could not spread, so they were never grafted.

cards.front: Which oenologist guided Cantina Santadi towards Terre Brune, first made in 1984?
cards.back: Giacomo Tachis (1933 to 2016), the oenologist of Tignanello.

questions.q: Terre Brune carries the word Superiore on its label. Under the DOC's rules, what must a Carignano del Sulcis Superiore come from?
questions.exp: The DOC's rules say the Superiore must come only from vines trained as alberello, bush vines; the old ungrafted Carignano of the sandy Sulcis is grown that way.

questions.q: In which year did Cantina Santadi make the first Terre Brune, with Giacomo Tachis advising?
questions.exp: Terre Brune was first made in 1984; the co-operative was founded in 1960, and the Carignano del Sulcis DOC dates from 1977.

sources.title: Cantina Santadi: Terre Brune
Cantina Santadi: Our story
AIS: disciplinare of the Carignano del Sulcis DOC
Wikipedia: Giacomo Tachis
The Drinks Business: Giacomo Tachis dies

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35 and one shared with Argiolas for Giacomo Tachis's dates; the co-operative's pages and sheet were read through search.

The plan's note is answered: the co-operative's own pages give 1984 for the first Terre Brune, and its sheet gives the grapes as Carignano 95 per cent and Bovaleddu 5 per cent, which agrees with the library's Carignano with Bovaleddu.

Tachis's arrival is dated by sources that disagree (the co-operative's page the mid 1970s, secondary accounts 1976 or 1980), so the story says only that he was brought in after the turn to bottled wine from the middle of the 1970s, as the co-operative tells it; the land reform board ETFAS behind the founding of 1960 rests on one source and is left out.

The claim that Terre Brune was the first Sardinian red of great structure aged in barriques is the co-operative's own, with one secondary beside it, and is hedged as its account; the release of the first vintage as late as 1988 rests on one source and is left out.

The DOC's rule that the Superiore comes only from alberello vines and its minimum of 85 per cent Carignano are read from the AIS copy of the 1977 disciplinare; its minimum ageing for the Superiore is unclear in the summaries read and is left out.
Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Antonello Pilloni, the co-operative's long serving president, named by its own pages.
Library and region record: p-cantina-santadi agrees; the region record's line for Carignano del Sulcis calls Terre Brune the benchmark, a word this record does not use.

records.place: Arzachena, Gallura, Isola dei Nuraghi IGT, north eastern Sardinia

wine.name: VT Vendemmia Tardiva
wine.classification: IGT, the geographic indication below DOC and DOCG
wine.grapes: Vermentino alone, from the estate's own vineyards.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyards around Arzachena in the Gallura hills of the north east, on granite soils among the granite outcrops of the district.
wine.making: As its name says, the Vermentino is picked late. It is fermented in stainless steel, then aged for some months in barriques and rested in bottle; the house releases it no earlier than two years after the harvest.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, yellow peach and candied lemon with fennel, almond and a light toast from the barrique; broad, creamy and dry, with a saline edge to its long finish.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, two years after the harvest, it keeps and deepens for many years in bottle, as the house intends.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; a young bottle gains from half an hour in a decanter; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: Vendemmia tardiva, late harvest: here a dry white from grapes picked late, not a sweet wine.
Sardinia's island wide geographic indication, which the house has long used in place of the Gallura DOCG.
The old name of the family estate, from the Latin caput erat, it was the capital, as the house tells it.

records.table: Capichera's VT Vendemmia Tardiva is a dry Vermentino from the granite of the Gallura, picked late and aged some months in barriques: broad, creamy and saline, with ripe pear, fennel and almond. It has the weight for a main course, poured cool rather than cold.
records.story: The Ragnedda family farmed land at Capichera, near Arzachena in the granite hills of the Gallura, and as the house tells it the name, from the Latin caput erat, it was the capital, is the old name of the family estate. In the late 1970s the family saw what Vermentino could do on its own and set out to bottle it unblended. The wine named Capichera was first made in 1980, and in the early 1980s, by its own account, the house turned wholly to the grape. In 1990 it made the first VT, Vendemmia Tardiva, from Vermentino picked late and, by the house's account, the first Vermentino vinified in barriques. Vign'angena followed in 1994, made at first from bought grapes until the young vineyards came of age. Vermentino di Gallura became a DOCG in 1996, Sardinia's only one, yet Capichera long labelled its whites Isola dei Nuraghi IGT, the island wide indication, rather than with the DOCG of its own district. Santigaìni, from a single plot, came in 2003. For a sommelier the VT shows Vermentino of the Gallura with weight, oak and years in bottle, and a candidate must remember that picked late here means dry.

others.name: Capichera

traps: Vendemmia tardiva on Capichera's VT means picked late, and the wine is dry, not a sweet late harvest white.
Capichera long labelled its whites Isola dei Nuraghi IGT rather than Vermentino di Gallura DOCG, though its vineyards lie in the Gallura itself.

cards.front: Capichera: what does VT stand for, and is the wine sweet?
cards.back: Vendemmia tardiva, late harvest; Capichera's VT is a dry Vermentino from grapes picked late.

cards.front: Capichera: which label has the house long used for its whites in place of the Gallura DOCG?
cards.back: Isola dei Nuraghi IGT, the geographic indication that covers the whole island.

questions.q: A guest expects Capichera's VT Vendemmia Tardiva to be sweet. What do you tell them?
opts: It is dry, from Vermentino picked late
It is sweet, from grapes dried on mats
It is fortified with grape spirit
It is a sparkling wine of late grapes
questions.exp: VT is vendemmia tardiva, late harvest, but Capichera makes it dry and ages it some months in barriques; it is neither a passito of dried grapes nor a fortified wine.

questions.q: In which year did Capichera make its first VT, by its account the first Vermentino vinified in barriques?
questions.exp: The VT dates from 1990; 1980 is the first year of the wine called Capichera, 1996 the year Vermentino di Gallura became a DOCG, and 2003 the first Santigaìni.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 35 and one shared with Argiolas for the Isola dei Nuraghi disciplinare; the house's pages were read through search.

Swap proposed, wine only: the house's own pages call the wine named Capichera, first made in 1980, its iconic wine, so the flagship the house leads with is the Capichera rather than the VT; the record is written on the plan's VT, which the library names first and the house dates to 1990, and the checker may move the pick to Capichera with the sources already in this record.

The appellation is unsettled by vintage: the house's 2023 page, Superiore.de and Vino.com give the VT as Isola dei Nuraghi IGT, while the house's 2024 page gives Vermentino di Gallura Superiore DOCG and Vino.com's 2024 listing still gives the IGT; the record gives the IGT and says the house has long used it.

The VT's oak is unsettled: the merchants give steel then 6 to 8 months in barriques (Vino.com, 2024) or about four months (Superiore.de, 2022 and 2023), with the malolactic in barrel on one sheet only, so the making says some months; one secondary says it is fermented and wholly aged in barriques, left out; the house's page gives a harvest in September or early October, the merchants late October, so the record says only that it is picked late.

Library tension: p-capichera's holdings say the estate is run by the Ragnedda family, but L'Unione Sarda reports its sale by the family to a Milanese buyer, a wine wiki giving 2022; the sale is left out of the story because the reports' addresses name living people and no other source gave the year.
Founded stays empty, as in the library: the house gives the late 1970s for its turn to unblended Vermentino and 1980 for its first wine, other accounts 1975 or 1981.
Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Mario Ragnedda and Alberto Ragnedda of the family, and the buyer, named Carlo Bonomi and Carlo Campanini Bonomi.
